content: Choosing running shoes starts with where you run. Road shoes have smooth soles and plenty of cushioning, while trail shoes have deeper lugs for grip on mud. Measure both feet in the afternoon, when they are at their largest, and leave a thumb's width in front of your longest toe. A gait check on a treadmill shows whether a neutral or a stability shoe suits you.

Most running shoes last between 300 and 500 miles. The midsole foam compresses long before the upper wears out, so look for creases in the foam, uneven wear on the outsole and new aches after easy runs. Rotating two pairs gives the foam time to recover and makes both pairs last longer.

Trail running shoes differ from road shoes in three ways: deeper lugs for grip, a rock plate to protect the foot, and a tougher upper. On hard-packed paths a road shoe is fine. On wet grass, mud and loose stone, a trail shoe gives far more grip and confidence on descents.

A couch to 5k plan takes a new runner from walking to running for 30 minutes in nine weeks. Week one alternates 60 seconds of running with 90 seconds of walking. Each week the running intervals get longer. Three sessions a week with a rest day between them is enough, and repeating a week is normal.

Training for a first 10k takes about eight weeks for someone who can already run 5k. The plan has three runs a week: one easy run, one run with faster intervals and one long run that grows by a kilometre each week. Keep the easy runs slow enough to hold a conversation.

The long run is the most important session in marathon training. It builds endurance and teaches the body to burn fat for fuel. Most plans build to a longest run of 20 miles three weeks before race day, then taper. Run it at an easy pace and practise taking on food and drink.

Eat a meal rich in carbohydrate two to three hours before a run: porridge, toast or a bagel work well. Avoid a lot of fat and fibre, which sit heavily in the stomach. For an early run, a banana 30 minutes beforehand is enough. Drink water through the morning instead of a large amount at once.

On runs longer than 90 minutes the body needs extra carbohydrate. Take an energy gel every 30 to 45 minutes with a few mouthfuls of water. In hot weather add electrolyte tablets to replace the salt lost in sweat. Practise in training so there are no surprises on race day.

Shin splints cause pain along the inner edge of the shin bone and usually follow a sudden jump in mileage. Rest from running for one to two weeks, ice the area and keep fit with cycling or swimming. Return gradually, check that your shoes are not worn out and add calf strengthening exercises.

Runner's knee is a dull ache around the kneecap that gets worse on stairs and downhill. Weak hips and quads are common causes. Cut back on mileage, avoid steep descents and strengthen the glutes and quads with squats and side leg raises. See a physiotherapist if it lasts more than a few weeks.
